Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Carlos had always moved through space with a dancer’s grace—aware of every angle, every surface, every body around him. That night, driving home from a late rehearsal, he was stopped at an intersection when a pickup truck blew through the red light and slammed into the driver’s side of his sedan. He remembers the sound more than the sight: the screech of tires, the explosive pop of metal crumpling, then the long, grinding scrape as his car spun. After that, silence, except for the hiss of a leaking radiator and his own ragged breathing. He was pinned for twenty minutes before emergency crews cut him free. He had not been severely injured physically, but something in him had been torn loose.

In the weeks that followed, Carlos found he could not put what had happened into words. When his wife, Elena, asked him about it, he would shrug or turn away—not from unwillingness, but because the event lived in him as a jumble of sounds and sensations, not a story he could tell. Sometimes, without warning, he would hear the screech of tires again, so vivid that he would flinch and look around, certain the crash was about to replay. Those moments left him soaked in a shame he could not explain: a conviction that the accident had happened because of the sort of person he was—careless, distracted, undeserving of good fortune. He started to believe that he would never feel normal emotions again, that the part of him that had once laughed easily and felt joy had been crushed in the wreck. A deeper helplessness settled in: he could not stop bad things from happening, so why bother trying?

His behavior shifted quietly at first. He began staying up until two or three in the morning, scrolling his phone or staring at the ceiling, because the moment he closed his eyes the sounds would start, and with them the shame. During the day, when a memory surfaced or a stressful moment arose, he would deliberately try to blank out—closing his eyes, going numb, leaving his body as if stepping behind a thick glass wall. He worked hard to suppress any thoughts of the crash, but the harder he pushed them away, the more the sounds ambushed him. He came to dread being touched unexpectedly; Elena’s hand on his shoulder could make him jerk away with a surge of alarm, and he would see the hurt in her face before he could explain. He started scanning every room he entered for exits, noting doors and windows automatically, even in his own home. In the dance studio, where he taught modern technique, the mirrors that once helped him refine his form now made him hyperaware of potential escape routes, and the accidental brush of a student’s hand during a partnering exercise sent his heart racing.

The consequences crept into his marriage and his work. Carlos began arriving late to rehearsals, claiming fatigue, then canceling classes because he felt too “off.” Elena, who had always been his softest landing, grew quietly distant; she did not know how to reach him when even a gentle touch startled him. He was haunted by the thought that he was failing her, failing his students, failing himself—and that this failure was simply another proof of his unworthiness. What finally drove him to seek help was a morning when he could not bring himself to unlock the studio door. He stood in the parking lot, scanning the exits, and knew he could not go in. He called a therapist from his car, his voice trembling. He was afraid of what he would find—afraid he would learn that he truly had lost his emotions forever, that the shame was deserved—but he was also desperately hoping that somewhere inside him, the dancer who felt music in his bones was still there, waiting to be touched again.
